ground_truth.title: ProxMox or Ubuntu or Debian for Windows virtualization?
ground_truth.author: slow-poke
ground_truth.main_content:
I want to install some yet to be determined flavor of Linux to be the main OS on a PC and then run Win7 and Win10 as virtual machines under Linux.
Older laptop; SSD is 1TB, and 32GB RAM, 2nd bay for another SSD but I don't think I need to use it.
Anyone here doing this and what would you suggest?

I'm running proxmox with ubuntu headless and Truenas as my main VM's. Within Ubuntu which has no GUI it is running docker which holds just about everything else , a windows 10 docker, plex, some media organizers, torrent client and a few other small things. surprisingly WINdows 10 as a docker container works well so far to run some cad software . the only somewhat involved part was getting my GPU shared into ubuntu, Nvidia is the only one supported atm that i know of so there is that .

The laptop.should be able to handle it no problem. proxmox has a learning curve but there is a ton of stuff on the net to help you along

I have used Debian for the past 15(?) years or so, with BeagleBone at work before I retired, and on my desktop there and at home since. I did run Windows 7 in VirtualBox back then with no significant issues that I recall. Debian claims to aim for stability, and does major updates much less frequently than other distributions which was one of the things I was looking for. Ubuntu is a downstream derivative of Debian, as are a number of others. Mostly, you may not notice much difference between them.

I've tried to install LinuxMint on my older WIN-7 workstation. Works reasonably well and has a desktop that mimics Windows.
I then installed WinBoat and in that WIN-10
Everything shows up as tabs or run one of the tabs which is the windows desktop.
And from that desktop I can run say Protel 99SE for PCB layout. But it is painfully slow. What takes a few seconds on WIN-10 is over a minute on this install. And a USB drive plugged in doesn't show up in the Windows file manager. Not sure how to fix that if I was going to put up with the slowness.

Oh and I was able to install GeoMagic which came after and then again before Alibre. I still have the dongle for it and it runs on the laptop with Windows but the USB pass through is still experimental so the dongle wasn't found. In fact after that it couldn't find the USB Dongle so I had to flip back to linuxmint and copy from the dongle into the documents folder which is shared with the WinBoat image.
GeoMagic ran reasonably well but the system has what was 15 years ago a high end NVIDIA GTX670. I assigned 3 of the 4 cores to the WinBoat and 8GB memory.

I think we chatted about this in one of the Win-10 end of life rants. I ended up installing Linux Mint on an old ex-Win-7 Laptop. It went quite smooth, just need to spend more time getting into it. It wont replace my Win-10 box for various reasons, but it doesn't owe me anything so figured why not learn 7 install some Linux apps. While researching Linux flavors I got a consistent vibe that Linux can only go so far on Nvidia graphics drivers because its basically closed source unless your name is MS. So even if you ran your Win app within a Linux shell, the GC was a potential troublemaker. This was consistent among gamers and CAD/Photo guys saying it was frustratingly close to Win installation but still had graphics glitches that weren't there before. Of course all depends.... So the advice was swap out your GC to one that Linux had a better chance of integrating if possible. And that potentially brings up new issues including cost.
My laptop came out in 2011. The advice was that it was so old, better odds that Linux probably had it figured out by now. It says 'all recommended graphics drivers are installed'. I have one irritating thing where one of the apps hides on the right margin so you wouldn't know it was there as though I had a 2nd monitor but improperly configured. I cant figure out how to make it stick on the one & only primary monitor, but I am a Linux sub-Novice. Asus Altec Lansing A53S, Intel Core i-7-2670QM CPU 2.2 GHz, ACPI X64 based PC, Nvidia Geforce 610M v359.46

I have several laptops and a desktop on mint. Works good and does what I need. Debian was what we used at work for all our back bone stuff.

I found this online:
The Driver Manager in Linux Mint is a built-in graphical tool (Menu > Administration > Driver Manager) that automatically scans your system and recommends proprietary drivers (like for NVIDIA/AMD graphics, Wi-Fi) for better hardware performance, offering easy one-click installation for optimal setup, though most hardware works out-of-the-box.
The system already knew what NVIDIA board I had. I changed it to now use High Performance. Then ran WinBoat and as soon as I ran GeoMagic it changed the screen resolution to 1024x768 and huge ICONs.
So now digging into that.
